title: Managing Long Running Tasks
subtitle: Work that takes seconds to hours — async job queues, workers, status tracking, retries, and progress reporting.
seoTitle: Design Managing Long Running Tasks | System Design Interview Breakdown
description: Work that takes seconds to hours — async job queues, workers, status tracking, retries, and progress reporting.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.text: Transcoding a video, generating a report, running user-submitted code, sending a million emails — some work simply takes too long to do inside an HTTP request. This pattern decouples **accepting** work from **doing** it, so users get an immediate response and the work completes reliably in the background.
If a request handler does a 5-minute job synchronously:

items: Clients and load balancers time out (often after 30-60 seconds).
A server crash loses the work with no record it was ever requested.
Spiky demand ties up web servers, so even fast endpoints slow down.
You can't scale the heavy work independently of the API.

blocks.title: Do it inline and raise the timeout

approach.text: Increase every timeout to 10 minutes and process the job in the request.

challenges.text: Doesn't survive crashes or deploys, holds connections and threads hostage, and still fails for jobs longer than the new limit.

blocks.title: Background threads on the web server

approach.text: Accept the request, spawn a background thread, and return immediately.

challenges.text: Work is lost if the server restarts, and web and worker load still compete for the same machines.

items: The API validates the request, writes a **Job** record (`status = PENDING`), enqueues a message, and returns `202 Accepted` with a job ID.
A separate pool of **workers** consumes the queue, marks the job `RUNNING`, does the work, and stores the result (often in blob storage) with `status = SUCCEEDED` or `FAILED`.
The client polls `GET /jobs/:id`, or is notified via webhook, SSE or push when it finishes.

approach.text: Workers scale independently on queue depth, and the queue's **visibility timeout** redelivers work if a worker crashes.

challenges.text: At-least-once delivery means jobs may run twice — make them idempotent. Very long jobs need heartbeats to extend their visibility timeout.

items: [ChatGPT](/learn/system-design/problem-breakdowns/chatgpt) — long LLM generations decoupled from the connection.
[Web Crawler](/learn/system-design/problem-breakdowns/web-crawler) — fetching and parsing pages at scale.

blocks.text: Workers periodically write progress (percent complete, current stage) to the job record or a fast store like Redis. Clients poll or subscribe via SSE. For multi-stage pipelines, model stages explicitly so progress is meaningful.
How do you handle failures and retries?

Retry transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter, up to a maximum attempt count, then move the job to a dead-letter queue and mark it `FAILED` with an error message. Distinguish retryable errors (timeouts) from permanent ones (invalid input) so you don't retry hopeless jobs.
How do you prevent one tenant or a burst from starving others?
Use separate queues or priorities (interactive vs. batch), per-tenant concurrency limits, and autoscaling on queue age rather than just depth.

Accept quickly, process asynchronously. Persist a job record, enqueue the work, let an independently scalable worker pool process it with retries and idempotency, and give clients a way to check status or be notified.

quiz.question: What should an API return when it accepts a long-running job?
options: 200 with the final result after waiting
quiz.explanation: The client gets an immediate acknowledgement and tracks the job by ID.

quiz.question: What redelivers a job if its worker crashes?
quiz.explanation: Unacknowledged messages become visible again for another worker.

quiz.question: Why must jobs be idempotent?
options: At-least-once delivery means a job may execute more than once

quiz.question: Why run workers separately from web servers?
options: So heavy work scales independently and doesn't slow the API
Web servers can't connect to queues
quiz.explanation: Independent pools let each side scale on its own load signal.
